Chat with Blowtorch to craft wild, singable lyrics and get them ready for amazing vocals, or use the tools: forge the lines, place the consonants, plan the runs, tune the vowels. Style ideas come from published analysis of gospel singing, including Mahalia Jackson. Nothing here imitates or synthesizes her voice.

The wavy underline marks the word to hold, with vibrato. A "run" tag marks a spot for a melisma. The meter checks only what can be measured from spelling and structure. It cannot tell you whether a line is good, and no tool can certify lyrics as perfect.

About the Mahalia Jackson reference

Her best-known recordings were mostly written by others. "Move On Up a Little Higher" was written by Rev. W. Herbert Brewster; her 1947 recording (Apollo, released December 1947) is described as the best-selling gospel song of all time, and Brewster credited her delivery. Thomas A. Dorsey, credited with more than 1,000 gospel songs, helped develop her career. So she is the example of how lyrics are delivered, more than a lyric author. Sales figures for it come from secondary sources and should be read as claims, not audited numbers.

The preset turns published descriptions of gospel craft into numbers: call and response between soloist and choir, repetition with improvised variation over a vamp, short interjections, a climb to a climax, short phrases and open vowels for held notes. The numbers are my starting estimates, not measurements of her songs. No lyrics were copied or analyzed, and the app does not write in her words.

Vowel space: F2 across, F1 down

F1 (jaw and tongue height)F2 (tongue front to back)harmonic lattice, green = within 25 cents

Each faint line is a harmonic of your sung note. Singers often tune F1 onto a harmonic so a vowel rings louder with less effort. Formant estimates get less reliable as pitch rises, because the harmonics become too sparse to outline the vocal tract. In tests on synthetic vowels the readings were close up to about 260 Hz (middle C) and tended to lock onto a harmonic from about 330 Hz (E4) upward, so treat higher notes as rough.

Lyric line

Bars show one beat per word: the colored start is the consonant before the beat, the purple middle is the vowel, the blue end is the release. Lead times are starting estimates to tune by ear. Spelling-based parsing is approximate: silent letters, soft c and unusual words can be misread.

Held note, then a run

The pitch guide is a plain synthesized tone for hearing the contour. It is not a voice model.

Settings

Method: learn the run on a consonant, keep it clean at 80 BPM, add 5 BPM per clean pass, then move to a narrow vowel and finally the lyric vowel.

What this is built on

Published analysis of Mahalia Jackson's recordings (HfM Weimar pop voices study) describes a vibrato near 6 to 7 Hz, a glide into long notes, runs of about 4 to 7 notes at the end of long notes, short phrases with breaths inside them, and almost entirely pentatonic note choice. Consonant and run practice follows common voice-teaching guidance. Formant tuning follows the harmonic-proximity idea in the Finding Resonance tool: distance from a formant to the nearest harmonic in cents.

Chat sends your messages and the conversation so far to Claude, on your own Claude account, each time you press Send. Lyric Forge sends your brief (theme, mood, vector settings and, for Refine, your current verse) only when you press Forge lyrics, Refine or Redo. Microphone audio is analysed in your browser and is never uploaded. Reference vowel values are approximate speech averages and shift in singing. This is a practice aid, not a substitute for a teacher.
